summary: Project SARS Amoeba turns NASA radar data into an open, bilingual web map that shows how water moves under Malaysia's monsoon clouds, exactly when ordinary satellite cameras are blind. For the November 2024 Kelantan flood, we processed six Sentinel-1 passes from NASA's OPERA products with a before-and-after change test. Our map shows about 20,300 ha of new flood water on 29 November and agrees with NASA's own water map (F1 0.75). About 244,000 people lived within 250 m of that water, and 4,100 ha stayed flooded for a week or more. For the 2026 Kedah rice season, we used NISAR's new L-band HH and HV data to watch paddy fields fill from 2% to 45% between late September and 1 November, weeks behind MADA's irrigation schedule in a drought year. NISAR found far more shallow field water than C-band radar, an open question we flag for ground checks. The project answers the challenge directly: why the surface changes, which polarizations show it, and what NISAR can do next. Anyone can click a spot to see its radar history, compare dates and analyze the trend via graph visualizations.
details:
What it does
Project SARS Amoeba is an open web map that shows where water is on the ground in Malaysia during the monsoon, when thick cloud blinds ordinary satellites. It uses radar, which sees through cloud day or night, to answer two questions:

  1. Where did Kelantan's November 2024 flood spread, and who lived beside it?
  2. Which of Kedah's MADA rice fields got water during the 2026 season?

How it works
A pipeline of 12 Python scripts searches NASA's catalogues and downloads only the data we need. It then:

  • Maps flood water. It compares radar passes before and during the flood. A pixel counts as new flood water only if it is dark now (VV below −15.5 dB) and at least 3 dB darker than before, on the same orbit track.
  • Follows the rice season. For Kedah, it uses NISAR's new L-band HH and HV channels to watch the fields fill.
  • Measures the impact. It counts hectares, how long water stayed, how many people live within 250 m, and rainfall. It also checks our maps against NASA's own water maps.

The results are baked into a static website that loads fast on any phone.

Results

  • On 29 Nov 2024, about 20,300 ha of new flood water across seven Kelantan districts.
  • About 244,000 people lived within 250 m of it.
  • 4,100 ha stayed flooded for a week or more, mostly in Tumpat and Pasir Mas.
  • In Kedah, rice land holding water rose from 2% on 23 Sep to 45% on 1 Nov 2026. Most fields got water only after MADA's third irrigation phase, weeks behind schedule in a drought year.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Disaster offices can see where water spread and who lives next to it.
  • MADA and agriculture officers can track which fields are actually getting water.
  • Insurers and researchers get an open, checkable record.

The map and the code stay free. Agencies would pay only for new regions, automatic updates and alerts. Running cost is under RM300 a month per region (our estimate). The next step is a one-season pilot with one Kelantan district office and one MADA region. Because NISAR covers almost all of Earth's land every 12 days, adding a new river or rice basin takes one config entry.

Tools and languages

  • Python: NumPy, rasterio, SciPy, pyproj, requests.
    • NASA: OPERA RTC-S1 and DSWx-S1 (Sentinel-1), NISAR L2 GCOV, NASA POWER rainfall, NASA GIBS imagery.
    • Others: ESA WorldCover, JRC Global Surface Water, WorldPop and DOSM district boundaries.
  • AI: we used Claude for brainstorming, research, data analysis and coding. The team reviewed every AI note, and no AI runs inside the page.
  • TypeScript and Vite: MapLibre GL, PMTiles, a COG tile protocol, a compare slider, Turf.js.
  • Hosting: Vercel, with the code on GitHub under an MIT licence.

What makes it creative

  • Swipe between a cloud-covered photo and radar to see "through" the cloud.
  • Click any spot to see its full radar history.
  • A map shows where water lingered.
  • One tap switches the whole interface to Bahasa Melayu.
  • Each district has an AI-written analysis. Code checks every number it quotes against our data.
  • Save a picture of any view, ready for a report.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about uncertainty: every number comes with a range, and we compare our maps with NASA's.
  • Known limits, stated openly: radar can't judge floods inside towns, and short floods can slip between passes.
  • Accessibility: two languages, works on phones, no login.
  • Reproducibility: every data granule ID is pinned, so anyone can re-run the pipeline with a free NASA Earthdata login.
  • Cost: a static site that is cheap to run.
  • Clear labelling: this is a student prototype, not an official flood warning.
